title: MC Escher and His Trippy Art
summary: Josh and Chuck profile M.C. Escher, the Dutch graphic artist known for tessellations, impossible staircases, and prints. They cover his early life in Leeuwarden and Arnhem, his rich father, his schooling in Delft and Haarlem, his mentor Samuel Jessurun de Mesquita, his travels in Italy and Spain (including the Alhambra), his marriage to Jetta, World War II and the loss of Mesquita, his woodcut, lithograph and mezzotint techniques, his math-inspired work and friendships with the Penroses, his late-career fame, and his death in 1972. Listener mail from Jenny closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Escher
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about room tone, then introduce M.C. Escher and his famous works such as the mirror sphere self-portrait and impossible staircases.

segments.title: Early life and education
segments.summary: Escher was born in Leeuwarden and grew up in Arnhem to a wealthy father, a civil engineer. He did poorly in school except math and drawing. His father pushed architecture, and at the Haarlem school he was mentored by Samuel Jessurun de Mesquita, who steered him toward graphic design.

segments.title: Travels in Europe, Italy and the Alhambra
segments.summary: Funded by his father, Escher traveled Europe in the early 1920s. He fell in love with the Italian countryside and was fascinated by Alhambra tilework and tessellations, which he later drew himself. He met his Swiss wife Jetta in Italy.

segments.title: World War II, exile, and Mesquita's fate
segments.summary: Escher moved his family from Italy to Switzerland and then Belgium, and later to the Netherlands after the Nazi invasion. Mesquita, a Jewish friend and mentor, was taken by the Nazis and killed. Escher kept a sketch of mosquitoes bearing a boot print. The hosts discuss his wartime experience and how it turned him inward.

segments.title: Style, dread, and the turn to inward inspiration
segments.summary: Losing Italy pushed Escher to invent subjects from imagination. His work featured severe angles and an unsettling mood. The hosts discuss his early experiments, his clown period, and his skulls and mummified priests.

segments.title: Woodcuts, lithographs, and mezzotints
segments.summary: The hosts explain Escher's printmaking. Woodcuts are carved in reverse, requiring multiple blocks for shading. Lithographs are drawn on limestone with grease and water chemistry, and Escher later destroyed or canceled the stones. Mezzotint, which he called the black art, was used for only a few works.

segments.title: Mathematics, tessellations, and the Penroses
segments.summary: After the war Escher became known mainly among scientists and mathematicians. He learned about the seventeen wallpaper groups, which the Alhambra contains, and befriended the Penroses. The Penroses' paper on impossible figures inspired his staircase prints. His Contrast/Order and Chaos piece and his Circle Limit works are discussed.

segments.title: Fame, exhibitions, and death
segments.summary: Escher's fame grew after exhibitions and articles in Time, Life, Scientific American and Rolling Stone, peaking with the counterculture. Stanley Kubrick reportedly tried to recruit him. He died of cancer at 73. The Brazil exhibition drew 70,000 visitors in 2011.

segments.title: Listener mail from Jenny
segments.summary: Jenny with an I writes that she has listened since 2011, that her son enjoys the show, and that children's science websites are a good way to find simple definitions. The hosts sign off.
